Segregation

/seg-rih-GAY-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Segregation means the practice or policy of keeping people or groups separate from one another, whether by race, age, category, or rule.

The factory enforces strict segregation of raw ingredients and finished products so that nothing contaminates the food heading out the door.

Worked Example

For decades, laws in the American South enforced the segregation of Black and white citizens in schools, buses, and restaurants, until the civil rights movement forced those laws down.

This is the word's most famous historical use: an official policy that kept two groups of people apart by law. Segregation applies to any enforced keeping-apart of groups, but this history gives the word real weight.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

separation: the state of being kept apart

isolation: being set apart, alone, from everyone else

quarantine: enforced separation to stop disease from spreading

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

integration: bringing groups together as one

inclusion: welcoming everyone into the same group

Where it sits · how officially it is enforced — separation → segregation → apartheid

separation vs. segregation: Separation is the neutral, everyday word for things simply being kept apart, with no policy behind it.

apartheid vs. segregation: Apartheid names an extreme, state-enforced system of racial segregation — far harsher and more specific than the general word.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — se-

Prefix — se-: apart, away (Latin, as in secede, seclude)

Root — greg

Root — greg: flock, herd (Latin grex, gregis)

Suffix — -ation

Suffix — -ation: act or process of

Put it together

Put it together: Put together, se- + greg + -ation literally means 'the act of setting apart from the flock' — pulling some members away from the herd and keeping them separate from the rest.

Use the root in a new word: congregate

Use the root in a new word: congregate: Fans began to congregate outside the stadium hours before the gates opened — gathering together like a flock.

Word Choice

formal / social policy

Segregation carries heavy historical weight from the era of legally enforced racial segregation, so use it thoughtfully — though in neutral technical contexts (segregation of chemicals, of age groups, of livestock) it simply means enforced separation of groups. Compare partition, also in this unit: you partition a single space or territory into sections; segregation keeps groups of people or animals apart from each other.
